title: Offered to all (Sifre Deuteronomy 343)
hook: midrash says God offered the Torah to other nations first
tomorrow: what did the world sound like when the voice spoke?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a God who is a fire, and a trail of errands to follow instead: clothe, visit, comfort, bury. Walk in His ways. Today, the moment those ways were handed over, and who else was asked.
screen: `WALK IN HIS WAYS.` → `WHO ELSE WAS ASKED?`

segments.voice: The group project gets offered around the table. Nobody wants to lead it. Then someone says fine, me, and from then on it's theirs. A midrash in the Sifre, on Moses' last blessing, tells Sinai a little like that. Before Israel, it says, God went to other peoples and offered the Torah. Each asked the same question: what's written in it? Each heard one command that cut against its own way of life, and said no. Then Israel was asked, and answered: we will do, and we will hear. So the answer to yesterday's question is: others. The Torah was offered to all.
screen: `OFFERED AROUND THE TABLE.` → `WHAT'S WRITTEN IN IT?` → `WE WILL DO, AND WE WILL HEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's that view in full. The blessing says the LORD came from Sinai, rose from Seir and shone from mount Paran, places tied in the Torah to other peoples. The Sifre reads it as God knocking on other doors first. Two things follow. The Torah was never a secret handed to one club; it was offered to the world. And Israel's yes was a choice, which is part of why it's worth keeping. Now the other voice. In tractate Shabbat, a sage named Rav Avdimi reads the verse where the people stand at the foot of the mountain, more literally under it, and pictures God holding the mountain over them like a barrel: accept, or this is your grave. That sounds like no choice at all, and the Talmud says so out loud: then the covenant could be challenged. Rava answers that they accepted it again, freely, in the days of Esther. So which is it, chosen or pressed? Both sit inside the tradition, and each guards something. The Sifre guards dignity: you said yes. The barrel guards honesty: some commitments feel bigger than you at the start, and the fully free yes can come later, when no one is holding a mountain. A parent could put it at dinner like this: you didn't pick where you started, and you still get to choose it.
screen: `GOD KNOCKS ON OTHER DOORS.` · `THE MOUNTAIN LIKE A BARREL.` · `ACCEPTED AGAIN, IN ESTHER'S DAYS.` · `CHOSEN, OR PRESSED?` · then, large: `OFFERED TO ALL.`

segments.voice: Find a pen and a scrap of paper. Write one thing you didn't pick but are choosing now: a family, a name, a promise, a practice. Under it, in a few words, write why you'd say yes to it today, and keep the paper somewhere you'll see it again.
screen: `ONE THING YOU DIDN'T PICK.` · `WHY YOU'D SAY YES TODAY.`

segments.voice: Offered to all: the Sifre's telling of Sinai. The Torah held out to other peoples first, and taken up by the one that said we will do, and we will hear.
Pocket this: offered to all. A yes you chose, even second, is a yes worth keeping.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching remembers Israel's answer at Sinai, na'aseh ve-nishma, 'we will do and we will hear', and the festival of Shavuot celebrates the giving of the Torah; the midrash that it was first offered to other peoples is retold in study and sermons.

chat.meaning: In the Sifre, the Torah was offered to others first, and Israel's yes made it theirs. A chosen yes is worth keeping.

Sifre.meaning: an early midrash on Numbers and Deuteronomy

Seir.meaning: hill country the Torah ties to Esau's descendants

Paran.meaning: a wilderness the Torah ties to Ishmael

Rav Avdimi.meaning: a sage quoted in the Talmud

Rava.meaning: a sage of the Babylonian Talmud

sources.ref: Sifre Deuteronomy 343 (on Deuteronomy 33:2: God offers the Torah to other peoples, who ask what is written in it and refuse)
Deuteronomy 33:2 (from Sinai, Seir and mount Paran)
Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 88a (Rav Avdimi bar Hama bar Hasa: the mountain like a barrel; Rav Acha bar Yaakov: a protest against the Torah; Rava: accepted again in the days of Ahasuerus, Esther 9:27)

notes: Sifre Deuteronomy 343 names specific peoples (the children of Esau, Ammon and Moab, Ishmael) and the command each refused, tied to its ancestor's story. The lesson deliberately keeps this general ('each heard one command that cut against its own way of life') so no people is cast as a foil. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable with that summary.
'Places tied in the Torah to other peoples': Seir with Esau (Gen 36:8), Paran with Ishmael (Gen 21:21). Confirm.

Shabbat 88a paraphrased: Rav Avdimi's barrel; the objection that this gives a strong protest against the Torah (Rav Acha bar Yaakov, here voiced as 'the Talmud says so out loud'); Rava's answer from Esther 9:27. Confirm attribution and phrasing.
Exodus 24:7 given as the literal 'we will do, and we will hear' (na'aseh ve-nishma), not quoted from JPS 1917 ('will we do, and obey').

Debate shape: the two views (the Sifre's free choice; the barrel and Rava's later free acceptance) are given in their own terms; the fork asks for the barrel story's best case. Practice kind: write a line by hand.
Family line: 'you didn't pick where you started, and you still get to choose it' offered as something a parent could say; confirm it reads as descriptive, not prescriptive.
